question: Explain why semantic landmark elements (header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer) matter beyond styling, then build the document skeleton of a blog post page using them correctly.
short:
**Semantic landmark elements expose an accessibility tree and document outline so screen-reader users can jump between regions and search engines can understand content hierarchy.**

- **One `<main>` per page:** it maps to the `main` landmark and wraps the dominant unique content.
- **Scoping rules:** `<header>` and `<footer>` at the document root map to `banner` and `contentinfo` landmarks; nested inside `<article>`/`<section>` they lose those roles.
- **`<article>` vs `<section>`:** use `<article>` for self-contained distributable content; use `<section>` for a thematic grouping that should normally have a heading.
answer:
Semantic elements carry **implicit ARIA roles** that build the browser's **accessibility tree**, letting screen-reader users jump between **landmarks** (banner, navigation, main, contentinfo) instead of reading the whole page linearly. They also give crawlers a clearer **content hierarchy** for SEO and make the markup self-documenting.

Key rules interviewers check:

- **One `<main>` per page** for the dominant unique content; it maps to the `main` landmark.
- **`<header>`/`<footer>` at the document root** map to `banner`/`contentinfo`; nested inside `<article>`/`<section>` they are scoped and lose those landmark roles.
- **`<nav>`** is for major navigation blocks (not every group of links).
- **`<article>`** is **self-contained and independently distributable** (a blog post, a comment, a card). **`<section>`** is a thematic grouping that should normally have a heading.
- **`<aside>`** is tangentially related content (sidebar, pull quote).

Using `<div>` for everything throws all of this away, forcing you to reconstruct meaning with ARIA later.

question: Explain how to make a form accessible and how native HTML validation works, then build a sign-up form that labels every control, groups related fields, and validates without JavaScript.
short:
**Accessible forms require every control to have a programmatically associated label, related controls grouped in `<fieldset>`/`<legend>`, and correct `type` + constraint attributes for native validation.**

- **Label association:** `<label for="id">` matched to the input's `id`, or wrap the input inside the `<label>`; placeholder is not a label substitute — it disappears on input.
- **Grouping radios/checkboxes:** `<fieldset>` + `<legend>` lets screen readers announce the group name alongside each option.
- **Native constraint validation:** `required`, `type="email"`, `pattern`, `minlength`, `min`/`max` block submission and surface accessible error messages; style states with `:valid`/`:invalid`.
answer:
Accessibility for forms rests on **programmatic association** between labels and controls, plus surfacing errors to assistive tech.

- **Labels**: use `<label for="id">` matched to the control's `id`, or wrap the control inside the `<label>`. Placeholders are **not** labels — they vanish on input and have poor contrast.
- **Grouping**: wrap a set of related radios/checkboxes in `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`; the legend is announced as the group's name.
- **Native validation (Constraint Validation API)**: attributes like `required`, `type="email"`, `pattern`, `minlength`, `min`/`max`, and `step` make the browser block submission and show built-in messages — no JS required. `:invalid`/`:valid` pseudo-classes let you style state.
- **Errors**: link a live error message with `aria-describedby` and mark the field `aria-invalid="true"` when you do custom validation.

Use the right **input type** (`email`, `tel`, `url`, `number`, `date`) so mobile keyboards adapt and validation comes for free.

question: Explain how a classic, async, and defer script differ in download and execution timing relative to HTML parsing, then place three scripts so an analytics beacon, a render-blocking polyfill, and an app bundle each load optimally.
short:
**A classic `<script>` blocks the HTML parser while it downloads and runs; `async` downloads in parallel and runs ASAP in arbitrary order; `defer` downloads in parallel and runs in document order after parsing.**

- **`async`:** best for independent, fire-and-forget scripts (analytics, ads) where order does not matter.
- **`defer`:** best for app bundles and anything that touches the DOM or depends on other scripts — runs in document order just before `DOMContentLoaded`.
- **When to block intentionally:** only for a polyfill that truly must execute before any other script.
answer:
All three start the same place in markup but interact with the parser differently:

- **Classic `<script src>`** (no attribute): the parser **pauses**, fetches, executes, then resumes. Blocks rendering — worst for performance unless intentional.
- **`async`**: fetched **in parallel** with parsing; executes **as soon as it arrives**, pausing parsing at that moment. **Order is not guaranteed**, so use it only for independent scripts (analytics, ads) with no dependencies.
- **`defer`**: fetched in parallel, but execution is **deferred until after the document is parsed** and runs **in document order**, right before `DOMContentLoaded`. Ideal for your app bundle and anything that touches the DOM or depends on other scripts.
- **`type="module"`** is `defer` by default.

Rule of thumb: **`defer` for app/dependency code, `async` for fire-and-forget**, and only block parsing for a polyfill that truly must run before everything else.
code:
<head>
  <!-- Must run before any other script; intentionally blocking -->
  <script src="/polyfills.js"></script>

  <!-- Independent, order does not matter: fire-and-forget -->
  <script src="https://cdn.example.com/analytics.js" async></script>

  <!-- App bundle: needs DOM + runs after parse, in order -->
  <script src="/vendor.js" defer></script>
  <script src="/app.js" defer></script>
  <!-- vendor.js is guaranteed to run before app.js -->
</head>

question: Explain the difference between resolution switching (srcset/sizes) and art direction (picture), then implement both so the browser picks the right file by viewport and device pixel ratio, and a different crop on small screens.

Provide candidates with **`srcset`** (using `w` width descriptors) and tell the browser the rendered width with **`sizes`**. The browser combines `sizes` with the viewport and **device pixel ratio** to choose the smallest sufficient file, saving bandwidth. This stays inside a single ``. - **Art direction** — a *different* image (crop, aspect ratio, or format) at different breakpoints. Use **``** with multiple **``** entries; the first matching `` wins, with `` as the mandatory fallback. - `` also enables **format negotiation**: serve AVIF/WebP with a JPEG fallback via `type`. Always keep a real `` inside `` (it is what actually renders and supplies `alt`), and pair with `loading="lazy"` for offscreen images.

question: Explain the role of metadata for SEO and social sharing, then write the <head> of a page with the essential meta tags, title, canonical link, and Open Graph / Twitter Card tags.
short:
**A well-crafted `<head>` stacks metadata for correct rendering, search visibility, and social sharing.**

- **Baseline:** `<meta charset="utf-8">` (first in `<head>`) and `<meta name="viewport">` are required on every page.
- **Search:** `<title>` is the most important on-page SEO signal; `<meta name="description">` drives click-through; `<link rel="canonical">` prevents duplicate-content dilution.
- **Social sharing:** Open Graph `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`, and `og:url` control the preview card on Facebook/LinkedIn/Slack; `twitter:card` covers X — the `keywords` meta tag is ignored by all major search engines.
answer:
Metadata lives in `<head>` and is invisible on the page but critical for discovery and sharing.

- **`<meta charset="utf-8">`** must come first (within the first 1024 bytes) so the parser decodes text correctly.
- **`<meta name="viewport">`** is required for responsive/mobile rendering.
- **`<title>`** is the single most important on-page SEO signal and the browser tab/label.
- **`<meta name="description">`** often becomes the search-result snippet (it is not a ranking factor but drives click-through).
- **`<link rel="canonical">`** tells search engines the authoritative URL, preventing duplicate-content dilution.
- **Open Graph (`og:*`)** controls the preview card on Facebook/LinkedIn/Slack; **Twitter Card (`twitter:*`)** does the same for X. Always set `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`, and `og:url`.

`<meta name="robots">` controls indexing. Avoid the long-dead `keywords` meta tag.
code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Understanding Semantic HTML | DevBlog</title>
  <meta name="description"
        content="A practical guide to semantic HTML, landmarks, and accessibility.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://devblog.example.com/semantic-html">
  <meta name="robots" content="index, follow">

  <!-- Open Graph (Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack) -->
  <meta property="og:type" content="article">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Understanding Semantic HTML">
  <meta property="og:description" content="A practical guide to semantic HTML.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://devblog.example.com/og.jpg">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://devblog.example.com/semantic-html">

  <!-- Twitter Card -->
  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
  <meta name="twitter:title" content="Understanding Semantic HTML">
  <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://devblog.example.com/og.jpg">
</head>

question: Explain what <!DOCTYPE html> does and what quirks mode is, then show markup that triggers standards mode versus a legacy snippet that would fall into quirks mode and why it breaks the box model.
short:
**`<!DOCTYPE html>` triggers standards mode so the browser follows current CSS specs; a missing or malformed doctype triggers quirks mode, which emulates 1990s legacy bugs.**

- **Standards mode:** the browser uses `content-box` by default; `width` is the content area only.
- **Quirks-mode box model:** `width` historically included padding and border (like `border-box`), so the same CSS produces different element sizes without the doctype.
- **Doctype placement:** it must be the very first thing in the document, before `<html>`; check the mode at runtime with `document.compatMode`.
answer:
The doctype is **not an HTML tag** — it is an instruction to the browser about which **rendering mode** to use:

- **`<!DOCTYPE html>`** (the short HTML5 doctype) triggers **standards mode (no-quirks)**, where the browser follows the current CSS/HTML specs.
- A **missing, misspelled, or legacy** doctype — or content before it — drops the document into **quirks mode**, which emulates 1990s browser bugs for backward compatibility.
- There is also **limited-quirks (almost-standards) mode**, mainly affecting inline-image baseline spacing in table cells.

The most cited quirks-mode difference is the **box model**: in quirks mode, `width` historically behaved like `box-sizing: border-box` (padding/border included), whereas standards mode uses `content-box` by default — so the same CSS produces different element sizes. The doctype must be the very first thing in the document, before `<html>`.

question: Explain the first rule of ARIA and when to reach for roles versus native elements, then build an accessible custom toggle button and contrast it with the markup you should have used instead.
short:
**The first rule of ARIA: don't use it if a native element provides the needed semantics and behavior.**

- **Native elements are free:** a `<button>` is focusable, fires on Enter/Space, and announces its role to assistive tech without any ARIA.
- **When ARIA is needed:** custom widgets require `role` (what it is), `tabindex="0"` (keyboard focus), state attributes (`aria-pressed`, `aria-expanded`), and manual key handlers — all things native elements give you for free.
- **ARIA changes only announcements, not behavior:** wiring up keyboard handling and keeping state in sync is always your responsibility.
answer:
**ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds **roles, states, and properties** to the accessibility tree, but it **changes only semantics — never behavior**. The **first rule of ARIA** is: *if you can use a native HTML element with the needed semantics and behavior, do that instead of repurposing a `<div>`*.

When you genuinely build a custom widget, you must supply everything the native element gave you for free:

- **`role`** to announce what it is (e.g. `role="button"`, `role="switch"`).
- **`tabindex="0"`** so it is keyboard focusable.
- **State** via `aria-pressed`/`aria-checked`/`aria-expanded`, kept in sync with JS.
- **Keyboard handlers** for Enter/Space, since a `<div>` does not fire click on those keys.

This is why a real `<button>` is almost always better: it is focusable, fires on Enter/Space, exposes the `button` role, and works with forms automatically.

question: Explain what custom data-* attributes are for and how the DOM dataset API maps to them, then implement an event-delegated list where each item carries data-* metadata read in JavaScript.
short:
**`data-*` attributes store custom private metadata on elements; the `dataset` API maps them to camelCased JS properties and they are queryable via CSS attribute selectors.**

- **`dataset` access:** `data-product-id` → `el.dataset.productId`; writing `el.dataset.selected = 'true'` updates the attribute; values are always strings.
- **CSS attribute selectors:** `[data-state="active"]` lets you style state without extra JS or classes.
- **Event delegation pattern:** one listener on the container reads `e.target.closest('[data-*]').dataset` — efficient and works for dynamically added items.
answer:
**`data-*` attributes** are a standards-compliant way to attach **custom, private metadata** to elements when there is no fitting native attribute — e.g. a record id, a state flag, or config for a JS component. They keep markup valid and avoid overloading `class`/`id` for data.

- The DOM surfaces them through the **`dataset`** property: `data-user-id` becomes `el.dataset.userId` (kebab-case to **camelCase**). Writing `el.dataset.userId = '5'` updates the attribute, and values are always strings.
- They are queryable in CSS via **attribute selectors** (`[data-state="active"]`) and readable with `getAttribute`.
- Common pattern: combine `data-*` with **event delegation** — one listener on the container reads the clicked item's dataset, which scales to dynamically added items.

Caveat: `data-*` is for client-side metadata, not sensitive data, and should not replace ARIA for accessibility state.

question: Compare localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies on lifetime, capacity, scope, and server visibility, then implement saving a user preference in localStorage versus an auth flag that must reach the server in a cookie.
short:
**`localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and cookies differ in lifetime, capacity, scope, and whether the server can see them — choose based on who needs the data and for how long.**

- **`localStorage`:** persists until cleared (~5-10 MB, client-only); best for UI preferences and non-sensitive caches that survive restarts.
- **`sessionStorage`:** scoped to one tab, cleared on close (~5 MB, client-only); best for per-tab transient state.
- **Cookies:** ~4 KB, sent on every matching HTTP request; use for auth/session tokens the server must read — always set `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite`; never store secrets in Web Storage.
answer:
All three persist data in the browser but differ sharply:

| | localStorage | sessionStorage | Cookies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Until cleared | Per tab/session | `Expires`/`Max-Age` |
| Capacity | ~5–10 MB | ~5 MB | ~4 KB |
| Sent to server | **No** | No | **Yes, every matching request** |
| JS access | Yes | Yes | Unless `HttpOnly` |
| Scope | Origin | Origin + tab | Domain/path |

Guidance:

- Use **localStorage/sessionStorage** for client-only state (theme, draft, UI prefs). They are synchronous and string-only (serialize objects with `JSON`).
- Use **cookies** when the **server** needs the value on each request — chiefly **session/auth tokens**, which should be `HttpOnly` (invisible to JS, mitigating XSS theft), `Secure` (HTTPS only), and `SameSite` (CSRF mitigation).
- Never put secrets in localStorage — any XSS can read it.

question: Explain the security risks of embedding third-party content in an iframe and what the sandbox attribute does, then embed untrusted content locked down with sandbox and a referrer/permissions policy.
short:
**By default an `<iframe>` can run scripts, submit forms, and navigate the parent window; `sandbox` applies a deny-by-default policy and you opt back in only what's needed.**

- **Bare `sandbox`:** no scripts, no forms, no popups, and the frame is treated as a unique opaque origin — maximum lockdown.
- **Re-enable selectively:** `allow-scripts`, `allow-forms`, `allow-popups`, `allow-same-origin` — grant only what the embed genuinely needs.
- **Critical warning:** combining `allow-scripts` and `allow-same-origin` for untrusted content lets the frame remove its own sandbox — never pair them for untrusted embeds.
answer:
An `<iframe>` loads a separate document that, by default, can execute scripts, submit forms, trigger downloads, open popups, and even try to **navigate the top-level window** (clickjacking/redirect risk). Embedding untrusted content without restriction is dangerous.

The **`sandbox`** attribute is a **deny-by-default** allowlist:

- `sandbox=""` (empty) blocks scripts, forms, popups, same-origin treatment, and top navigation — the frame is placed in a **unique opaque origin**.
- You **re-enable** specific powers with tokens: `allow-scripts`, `allow-forms`, `allow-popups`, `allow-same-origin`, `allow-top-navigation`.
- **Caution**: combining `allow-scripts` **and** `allow-same-origin` lets the frame remove its own sandbox, so avoid pairing them for untrusted content.

Complement it with **`allow`** (Permissions Policy: gate camera/geolocation), **`referrerpolicy`** to limit leaked URLs, and **`loading="lazy"`** for offscreen frames. CSP `frame-src`/`frame-ancestors` adds a further layer.
code:
<!-- Locked-down embed of untrusted content -->
<iframe
  src="https://widgets.example.com/embed"
  title="Third-party rate widget"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"
  allow="geolocation 'none'; camera 'none'"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
  loading="lazy"
  width="320" height="200">
</iframe>

<!-- Note: we did NOT add allow-same-origin alongside allow-scripts,
     so the frame cannot escape its own sandbox. -->

question: Explain how block, inline, and inline-block boxes differ in flow, sizing, and box-model behavior, then build a row of nav links where setting width/padding actually takes effect.
short:
**Block elements stack vertically and fill available width; inline elements flow in text and ignore `width`/`height`; inline-block flows inline but honors box dimensions — the hybrid for sized items in a row.** - **Block** (`
`, `

`):** starts on a new line, fills the available width, and respects all box-model properties including vertical margins. - **Inline** (``, ``):** flows within a line; `width`/`height` are ignored and top/bottom margins do not affect surrounding layout. - **Inline-block:** sits next to siblings but accepts `width`, `height`, and vertical padding/margin; note that whitespace between tags creates small rendering gaps.
answer:
The `display` value controls how a box participates in flow:

- **`block`** (`div`, `p`, `section`): starts on a new line, fills the available width, and **respects** `width`, `height`, and all margins/padding.
- **`inline`** (`span`, `a`, `em`): flows within a line like text. It **ignores `width`/`height`**, and **top/bottom margins don't move surrounding content** (vertical padding overflows visually without affecting layout). Multiple inline elements sit side by side.
- **`inline-block`**: a hybrid — it **flows inline** (sits next to siblings) but behaves as a block internally, so `width`, `height`, and vertical padding/margins **work**. Classic use: nav items or buttons you want inline but sized.

A subtlety: inline and inline-block boxes are affected by whitespace in the source (the rendered gaps) and by `vertical-align`. Today fl/grid often replace inline-block, but it remains a common interview topic.

question: Explain when to choose canvas versus SVG (immediate vs retained mode, DOM access, scaling, accessibility), then draw the same circle in both and explain the trade-offs of each implementation.
short:
**SVG is retained-mode vector DOM — scalable, styleable with CSS, natively accessible; Canvas is immediate-mode pixels — fast for high-frequency rendering but not a DOM and not accessible by default.**

- **SVG:** each shape is a DOM node with events, CSS, and optional ARIA; vector so resolution-independent; performance degrades with very many elements.
- **Canvas:** shapes are drawn as pixels via JS and forgotten — hit-testing, animation, and accessibility are entirely manual; ideal for games, data-dense visualizations, and image processing.
- **Rule:** few interactive scalable elements → SVG; thousands of objects or real-time pixel work → Canvas.
answer:
Both render graphics but use opposite models:

- **SVG (retained mode)**: each shape is a **DOM node**. It is **vector**, so it scales to any resolution without blur; elements are **styleable with CSS**, **individually scriptable** (attach events), and **accessible** (add `<title>`, `role`, `aria-label`). Great for **icons, logos, diagrams, and charts** with a manageable element count. Many thousands of nodes get slow because each is a DOM object.
- **Canvas (immediate mode)**: a single bitmap you draw into with a JS API. There is **no DOM** for individual shapes — once drawn, pixels are forgotten, so you redraw to animate, and hit-testing/accessibility are manual. It is **fast for huge numbers of objects**, pixel manipulation, and **games/visualizations**, but it is **resolution-dependent** (needs DPR scaling to stay crisp).

Rule of thumb: **few, interactive, scalable elements → SVG; many, pixel-heavy, high-FPS → canvas.**
code:
<!-- SVG: vector, in the DOM, scalable, accessible, CSS-styleable -->
<svg width="100" height="100" role="img" aria-label="Blue circle">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="steelblue" />
</svg>

<!-- Canvas: immediate-mode pixels, drawn via JS, no per-shape DOM -->
<canvas id="c" width="100" height="100"></canvas>
<script>
  const ctx = document.getElementById('c').getContext('2d');
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.arc(50, 50, 40, 0, Math.PI * 2); // x, y, radius, start, end
  ctx.fillStyle = 'steelblue';
  ctx.fill();
  // To animate, you must clearRect + redraw each frame.
</script>

question: Explain how to embed video accessibly and with cross-browser fallbacks, then build a <video> with multiple sources, captions, a poster, and the attributes that govern autoplay behavior.
short:
**Accessible video embedding combines multiple `<source>` formats for codec fallback, a `<track kind="captions">` for deaf/hard-of-hearing users, a `poster` image, and correct autoplay flags.**

- **Format fallback:** list `<source>` elements best-format-first (WebM then MP4); text inside `<video>` is the last-resort browser fallback.
- **Captions:** `<track kind="captions" srclang="en" src="clip.vtt" default>` is the key accessibility requirement — it serves deaf/HoH users and quiet/noisy environments.
- **Autoplay rules:** browsers block autoplay with sound; pair `autoplay` with `muted` (and `playsinline` on iOS) — and add explicit `width`/`height` plus `controls` for keyboard-accessible playback.
answer:
Accessible, robust video embedding combines fallbacks, captions, and correct playback flags:

- **Multiple `<source>`**: list formats best-first (e.g. WebM then MP4); the browser uses the first it can play, with text inside `<video>` as the last-resort fallback.
- **Captions / subtitles**: add `<track kind="captions" srclang="en" src="….vtt" default>` (WebVTT) so deaf/hard-of-hearing users and noisy/quiet environments are served — this is the key accessibility requirement, alongside `<track kind="descriptions">` where relevant.
- **`poster`**: a placeholder image shown before playback.
- **`controls`**: expose native, keyboard-accessible controls.
- **Autoplay rules**: modern browsers **block autoplay with sound**. To autoplay you must add **`muted`** (and usually **`playsinline`** so iOS doesn't go fullscreen); add `loop` for background video. Avoid `preload="auto"` on data-sensitive pages.

Always give the video a clear surrounding label/heading and avoid autoplaying content that moves for more than 5s (WCAG).
